Do NOT use it for code review, design-doc auditing, cross-file consistency checks, or open-ended analysis — it reads excerpts rather than whole files and will miss content past its read window. - dataviz: Use this skill whenever you are about to create ANY chart, graph, plot, dashboard, or data visualization, in ANY output medium — an HTML or React artifact, inline SVG, plotting code in any library (matplotlib, plotly, d3, Recharts, …), an image/PNG you will render and upload, or a chart shared into Slack. Read it BEFORE writing the first line of chart code, choosing chart colors, building a stat tile / meter / KPI row, or laying out a dashboard. Produces visualizations that read as one system — elegant, accessible, consistent in light and dark — using a brand-neutral placeholder palette you swap for your own. Teaches a design-system-agnostic method: a form heuristic, a color formula with a runnable validator, mark specs, and interaction rules. A validated default palette is documented in `references/palette.md` — swap that file's values for your brand's. Triggers on: "chart", "graph", "plot", "data viz", "visualization", "dashboard", "analytics", "visualize data", "categorical colors", "sequential / diverging palette", "stat tile", "sparkline", "heatmap", "legend", "axis", "tooltip", "chart colors", "color by series".
- update-config: Use this skill to configure the Claude Code harness via settings.json. Automated behaviors ("from now on when X", "each time X", "whenever X", "before/after X") require hooks configured in settings.json - the harness executes these, not Claude, so memory/preferences cannot fulfill them. Also use for: permissions ("allow X", "add permission", "move permission to"), env vars ("set X=Y"), hook troubleshooting, or any changes to settings.json/settings.local.json files. Examples: "allow npm commands", "add bq permission to global settings", "move permission to user settings", "set DEBUG=true", "when claude stops show X". For simple settings like theme/model, suggest the /config command.
- keybindings-help: Use when the user wants to customize keyboard shortcuts, rebind keys, add chord bindings, or modify ~/.claude/keybindings.json. Examples: "rebind ctrl+s", "add a chord shortcut", "change the submit key", "customize keybindings".
- simplify: Review the changed code for reuse, simplification, efficiency, and altitude cleanups, then apply the fixes. Quality only — it does not hunt for bugs; use /code-review for that.
- fewer-permission-prompts: Scan your transcripts for common read-only Bash and MCP tool calls, then add a prioritized allowlist to project .claude/settings.json to reduce permission prompts.
- loop: Run a prompt or slash command on a recurring interval (e.g. /loop 5m /foo, defaults to 10m) - When the user wants to set up a recurring task, poll for status, or run something repeatedly on an interval (e.g. "check the deploy every 5 minutes", "keep running /babysit-prs"). Do NOT invoke for one-off tasks.
- claude-api: Reference for the Claude API / Anthropic SDK — model ids, pricing, params, streaming, tool use, MCP, agents, caching, token counting, model migration.
TRIGGER — read BEFORE opening the target file; don't skip because it "looks like a one-liner" — whenever: the prompt names Claude/Anthropic in any form (Claude, Anthropic, Fable, Opus, Sonnet, Haiku, `anthropic`, `@anthropic-ai`, `claude-*`, `us.anthropic.*`, `[1m]`); the user asks about an LLM (pricing/model choice/limits/caching) — never answer from memory; OR the task is LLM-shaped with provider unstated (agent/MCP/tool-definition/multi-agent/RAG/LLM-judge/computer-use; generate/summarize/extract/classify/rewrite/converse over NL; debugging refusals/cutoffs/streaming/tool-calls/tokens).
SKIP only when another provider is being worked on (overrides all triggers): OpenAI/GPT/Gemini/Llama/Mistral/Cohere/Ollama named in the query; OR `grep -rE 'openai|langchain_openai|google.generativeai|genai|mistralai|cohere|ollama'` over the project hits (run this grep FIRST if no provider named — don't Read the file).

1. Whether such middleware exists at all.
2. If it exists, the file path(s) where it's defined and where it's registered/applied to routes.
3. Any configured request limits (e.g., requests per minute/second, window size) and whether it's actually "per-user" (keyed by user ID) vs per-IP or global.

content.text:
`golang.org/x/time` is only an indirect (transitive) dependency — not imported or used anywhere in the codebase.

## Findings

**1. Does per-user API rate-limiting middleware exist? No.**

I searched the entire repository (Go backend under `server/`, `internal/`, `store/`, plus the `web/` frontend) for `rate limit`, `ratelimit`, `rateLimiter`, `throttle`, `limiter`, `429`/`TooManyRequests`, and related terms. No rate-limiting middleware, interceptor, or handler of any kind is implemented anywhere in this codebase.

**2. What actually exists (middleware/interceptor registration):**

This is a Go backend (looks like the "memos" project) using [connectrpc](https://connectrpc.com/) rather than Express/Koa/Fastify. Its middleware equivalent is a chain of Connect RPC interceptors, registered in:

- `/bench/repo/server/router/api/v1/v1.go` (lines ~133-141) — registers the interceptor chain:
  ```go
  connectInterceptors := connect.WithInterceptors(
      NewMetadataInterceptor(), // Convert HTTP headers to gRPC metadata first
      NewLoggingInterceptor(logStacktraces),
      NewRecoveryInterceptor(logStacktraces),
      NewAuthInterceptor(authorizer),
  )
  ```
- `/bench/repo/server/router/api/v1/connect_interceptors.go` — defines `MetadataInterceptor`, `LoggingInterceptor`, `RecoveryInterceptor`, and `AuthInterceptor`. None of these implement request throttling/rate limiting — they handle header-to-metadata conversion, logging, panic recovery, and authentication/authorization only.

There is no throttling step in this chain, no login-attempt/brute-force lockout logic (checked `server/router/api/v1/auth_service_session.go`, `server/auth/authenticator.go`), and no reverse-proxy config (no nginx/Caddy conf files) that might apply rate limiting at the infrastructure layer.

**3. Configured limits: none exist to report.**

- No requests-per-minute/second or window-size configuration found anywhere.
- No per-user (keyed by user ID), per-IP, or global request-rate limiting is implemented.
- The only related material in the repo is documentation/example code, not a wired-up feature:
  - `/bench/repo/internal/email/README.md` (lines 286-295) shows an *example* snippet recommending emails be rate-limited using `golang.org/x/time/rate`'s `rate.NewLimiter(rate.Every(time.Second), 10)` — but this is just illustrative docs for email sending, not implemented, and unrelated to API request middleware.
  - `/bench/repo/internal/email/doc.go` (line 86) has a one-line comment "Rate limit email sending to prevent abuse" as a suggested best practice, again not implemented.
  - `golang.org/x/time v0.15.0` appears in `go.mod`/`go.sum` but only as an **indirect** transitive dependency — grepping the whole codebase shows it is never imported in any `.go` file, so it isn't backing any actual rate limiter.

**Conclusion:** There is no per-user (or per-IP, or global) API rate-limiting middleware anywhere in this repository. The connect-RPC interceptor chain that serves as this project's middleware layer only handles metadata conversion, logging, panic recovery, and auth — no throttling logic exists at the application or proxy level.
